newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK "Pillar of Shame" democracy sculpture rejected.
newsitem.headline: HK "Pillar of Shame" democracy sculpture rejected.

text.p: Democracy activists stormed out of a Hong Kong municipal council meeting on Tuesday after officials rejected a request to display a sculpture symbolising the fight for human rights when the territory returns to China.
The Urban Council voted by 18 to 13 against a request by the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Democratic Movements in China to exhibit the "Pillar of Shame" sculpture.
However, the council approved an application to hold a pro-democracy forum in central Hong Kong on June 30, the eve of the handover.
The sculpture was created by Danish artist Jens Galschiot, who is displaying his work in places which he thinks face political oppression.
The work portrays 50 human bodies twisted into a six-metre (20-foot) high pillar, weighing two tonnes, symbolising oppression.

Alliance members, who wanted to put the sculpture on show in a park from June to September, donned white surgical masks daubed with the words "political censorship" and stormed out of the meeting after the setback.
Urban Councillor Stanley Ng, a spokesman of the Democratic Party, said councillors who voted against the request had bowed to self-censorship.
"It's obvious that it (the issue) was under heavy political lobbying and they carried out self-censorship," Ng told Reuters.
"They claimed the Pillar Of Shame is a political work of art and they don't want to allow it to be displayed. They see it as clashing with the reunification of Hong Kong and China."
Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, and many organisations have planned events to mark the occasion.

Democracy activists view the Urban Council's rejection of the sculpture as a sign that authorities are already bowing to China's views on the democracy movement. Beijing deems the alliance subversive.

Future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa has launched plans, inspired by China's parliament, to curb civil liberties after the handover, with a ban on foreign political funding and new limits on the right to protest.
